```md Documents/rock_proposal.md
# Proposal: Automated Production Deployments

## Executive Summary

This proposal describes changes to our process of deploying code to production.
These changes should result in time savings, a better developer experience, and
fewer errors when deploying code.

## Motivation

Here's the current state of affairs:

All code for a client lives in a single Git repo. There is a folder for each
NetSuite account. In the case of Solution Source, that is a folder for
Production and a folder for Sandbox.

When writing code, we edit the files in the sandbox folder and upload to the
sandbox account as we work. When we are confident the code is working as it
should, we get a code review and commit our changes. When the time comes to
deploy the code to production, we first copy and paste the contents of all files
changed in the sandbox to

the sister file in the production folder. Then we commit these changes. Finally,
we upload these updated files in the production folder to the production account
using the VS Code extension, or sometimes an Account Configuration Project
(ACP). (Sometimes steps two and three are swapped, but you get the idea.)

This has a few drawbacks:

1. We can never be confident that the code in our Git repos matches the code in
   the corresponding account. Finding code in an account that is not in source
   control is not uncommon. I also often forget to upload code changes made
   during a code review.
2. Leaving aside the process of actually uploading code, just moving code in our
   Git repos from sandbox to PROD is time-consuming and error prone.
3. We risk uploading code to the wrong account. It is up to individual
   developers to be careful enough to avoid taking down a production account
   with a bad upload.
4. It is easy to overwrite changes made by another developer to a file you are
   working on. Checking to make sure this doesn't happen is a time-consuming
   process, and not enforced.
5. If we want to introduce TypeScript, it isn't clear how we will add
   compilation to our process.
6. If we want to introduce tools such as a linter, a formatter, or a unit test
   framework, it's not clear how we would enforce running those tools before
   deployment, nor how to mandate that those checks pass before deployment.

This proposal is a recommendation for reworking our production deployment
process. While I think it could be very valuable to rework our development
process as well, most changes to our developement process can happen
independently of changes to our production deployment process. Therefore, the
vast majority of suggested development process changes will be outlined in a
separate proposal.

## Proposed Process Change - Overview

### Git Repo Structure and Permissions

Every client will have one repo for their NetSuite code. Each repo will have one
branch for each account. I recommend:

- `main` - Production account
- `dev` - development sandbox
- `test` - test sandbox, when applicable

This also means that we will no longer have "Client Name Sandbox" and "Client
Name Production" folders in our repos. Production code will live in the
production branch, development code will live in the development branch, etc.

Additionally, the branch for the production account (`main` in this example)
will have permissions set such that nobody can push directly to `main`, except
perhaps for select senior devs or SEs. Everybody else will need to open a pull
request in order to get their code changes into `main`.

### Development Process

For the purpose of this proposal, our development process would look almost
identical. Parts that are different are emphasized:

1. _Check out the correct branch (`dev`)_
2. Pull changes
3. Make your changes, and upload them to the dev sandbox using VS Code
4. When Changes are complete, get them code reviewed
5. _After code review, commit and push your changes to the `dev` branch_

The only difference here is that we are pulling from and pushing to the `dev`
branch instead of `main` or `master`.

### Deployment to Production

Every time code is pushed or merged into `main`, it will automatically be
deployed to the corresponding production account. This is the reason for the
branch restrictions on `main`. The vast majority of the time, we will want to
use PRs to move code from `dev` or `test` to `main`.

Here's a more detailed breakdown of the proposed process:

1. Open a PR from the `dev`(or `test`) branch to the `main` branch. Add any
   necessary documentation to the PR.
2. Run the following automated checks as soon as the PR is opened:
   1. Compare code in account with the code we deployed last. Also compare the
      last deployed script objects to the script objects in the account. They
      should be identical. If they are not, someone has made a chance directly
      in the production account and we should not deploy. Any conflicts will
      need to be resolved manually.
   2. (_optional_) Other checks can be inserted here later if desired. These
      could include unit tests and/or linter checks. The additional checks could
      also happen before the comparison if that makes more sense.
3. Request at least one review for the PR.
4. If the checks from step 2 pass and the PR has been approved, we can merge the
   code into `main`.
5. Merging code into `main` will trigger a deployment:
   1. Run the file compare check from step 2 again. Something could have changed
      between when we opened the PR and when we merge it. If the comparison
      finds conflicts, abort the deployment.
   2. Deploy the changes via ACP. This should include SuiteScript files and
      their corresponding objects.

## Expected Benefits

### Improved Developer Productivity

Developers will no longer need to:

- Copy code from the sandbox folder to the production folder
- Manually compare and upload each file
- Create and configure script records & deployments

### Fewer Mistakes

The tasks described above are not only time-consuming. They are also
error-prone. With this new process, we no longer need to worry about:

- Forgetting to upload a file
- Forgetting to compare a file before uploading
- Uploading files to the wrong account.
- Forgetting to create or correctly configure script records or deployments

### Better value for clients

By making developers more efficient and drastically reducing the set of possible
mistakes, we can provide a better experience to our clients and increase their
confidence in our customization services.

## Implementation Details

### Tooling

I evaluated two platforms for automating deployments: BitBucket Pipelines and
Mint CI/CD from RWX. There are pros and cons to each.

| Bitbucket Pipelines                                 | Mint CI/CD                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| We already have access to this                      | Requires new RWX accounts for each dev                     |
| Limited caching options                             | All steps are cached if possible, with no config necessary |
| 2500/3500 build minutes per month depending on plan | Unlimited - Billed per second                              |
| Requires custom docker images                       | Built-in caching eliminates the need for custom images     |
| Built-in to BitBucket                               | Currently does not have a BitBucket Integration            |

My proof of concept uses Mint for the build logic, and this can be triggered
with Mint's GitHub integration or by using BitBucket Pipelines to trigger a Mint
built via the Mint CLI. My recommendation is to stick with Mint for reasons I'll
list below.

Despite my best efforts, I was unable to get an implementation of the deployment
process to work with BitBucket Pipelines. I'm sure it is possible, but I kept
running into issues with Docker containers. Containers are necessary in order to
avoid installing dependencies like Java, Node.js, suitecloud-cli, etc. on each
run. I was able to get docker images working on my machine, but then things
wouldn't behave right on Bitbucket pipelines. I'm not sure whether this is an
issue with my Docker image or an issue with Pipelines.

Additionally, I had trouble getting the suitecloud java cli working on a docker
image with an Alpine base. I got it working on Ubuntu instead. Unfortunately,
this means we now have an 800MB+ image to download for every run. These
inefficiencies slow down the process and also use more of our limited build
minutes.

While there will be some effort involved in setting up Mint to work for us, I
suspect that it will save us time in the long run. Managing Docker images would
be an ongoing maintenance task that would add up over time.

Mint doesn't have an integration with BitBucket at the moment. This could change
in the future, as the product is still young. We can work around this and keep
our repos on BitBucket by using BitBucket Pipelines to trigger a Mint build via
the Mint CLI. To fully isolate client accounts, we would need to create a new
RWX account for deployment for each client, a step that wouldn't be necessary
with GitHub. The BitBucket pipeline that triggers the Mint run will also always
be successful, meaning we will need to hop over to Mint to see the actual status
and results. We also wouldn't be able to block PRs to `main` using this flow.

For that reason, I suggest that when we try this, we add a GitHub remote to our
repo and push to GitHub for deployments. PRs would be created in GitHub too. If
we don't run into any issues using GitHub, I'd suggest we consider moving all of
our repos over. GitHub's servers seem to be many times faster than BitBucket's,
so there is a benefit here regardless of whether we continue to use Mint.
However, In the short term we can just use a GitHub repo in conjunction with our
BitBucket repo while testing.

### Git Branch Permissions

BitBucket and GitHub both allow you to disable pushing to specific branches. I
know BitBucket allows you to add exceptions for particular users, and I'd be
shocked if GitHub didn't also have that option. I would suggest that we only
allow a select few, if any, to push directly to main. This would allow more
senior devs to push quick fixes if necessary, but would require any other
changes to go through the standard review process.

### NetSuite Permissions

I'm not sure whether this is possible, but it might be worth considering whether
we should revoke token access to production accounts for devs. This would force
us to go through the process for deploying code to production. However, even if
we don't do this we have a strong incentive to avoid manual uploads, as manual
uploads will break future automated deployments.
```

Here's a more concise version that maintains the key points:

```markdown
# Proposal: Automated Production Deployments

## Executive Summary
This proposal outlines changes to our code deployment process to improve efficiency, developer experience, and reduce deployment errors.

## Current Problems
1. Code in Git repos often doesn't match NetSuite accounts
2. Manual sandbox-to-production code migration is error-prone
3. Risk of uploading to wrong accounts
4. Easy to overwrite others' changes
5. Unclear implementation path for TypeScript, linting, and testing

## Proposed Solution

### New Repository Structure
- One repo per client with branches for each account:
  - `main` (Production)
  - `dev` (Development sandbox)
  - `test` (Test sandbox)
- Restricted permissions on `main` branch
- Elimination of separate Production/Sandbox folders

### Automated Deployment Process
1. Create PR from `dev` to `main`
2. Automated checks:
   - Compare account code with last deployment
   - Run optional tests/linting
3. Require code review
4. Upon approval and passing checks, merge triggers automatic deployment

## Benefits
- Eliminates manual file copying and uploads
- Prevents common deployment errors
- Reduces risk of wrong account uploads
- Ensures proper script record configuration

## Technical Implementation
Recommended: Mint CI/CD over BitBucket Pipelines
- Better caching
- Per-second billing
- No custom Docker image maintenance
- Requires GitHub integration for optimal functionality

## Required Changes
- Set up branch permissions
- Create deployment automation
- Consider revoking direct production access tokens
```

The original was detailed but contained some redundant information and overly specific implementation details. This version focuses on the core proposal while maintaining all crucial information for decision-making.

```markdown
- One repo per client with branches:
  - `main` - Production
  - `dev` - Development sandbox
  - `test` - Test sandbox (when applicable)
- Restricted push access to `main`
- Elimination of separate Production/Sandbox folders

### Development Process
1. Work in `dev` branch
2. Pull changes
3. Make and upload changes to dev sandbox
4. Get code review
5. Commit and push to `dev`

### Automated Deployment Flow
1. Create PR from `dev` to `main`
2. Automated checks:
   - Compare account code with last deployment

3. Code review
4. Upon approval and passing checks, merge triggers deployment

## Technical Implementation Details

### Platform Comparison

| Bitbucket Pipelines | Mint CI/CD |
|---------------------|------------|
| Existing access | Requires new RWX accounts |
| Limited caching | Comprehensive caching |
| 2500/3500 monthly build minutes | Pay-per-second billing |
| Requires custom docker images | No custom images needed |
| Native BitBucket integration | Requires GitHub integration |

### Implementation Recommendations
1. Use Mint CI/CD for build logic
2. Add GitHub remote for deployments
   - Faster servers than BitBucket
   - Better PR blocking capabilities
   - Consider full migration if successful

### Permission Management
- BitBucket/GitHub: Restrict `main` branch pushes
- Exception access for senior developers
```

2. Removes redundant explanations

You make a good point. The outline is cleaner, but it loses important context that helps stakeholders fully understand the proposal. Here's how I'd revise it to include necessary detail while maintaining clear organization:

```markdown
# Proposal: Automated Production Deployments

## Executive Summary
This proposal outlines changes to our production deployment process to improve efficiency, reduce errors, and enhance developer experience.

## Current State and Problems
Currently, all client code lives in a single Git repo with separate folders for each NetSuite account (Production and Sandbox). Developers:
1. Edit sandbox folder files and upload to sandbox
2. Get code review and commit changes
3. Copy/paste sandbox changes to production folder files
4. Commit these changes
5. Upload updated production files to the production account

This workflow leads to several problems:
1. Code in Git repos often doesn't match NetSuite accounts due to:
   - Missed uploads after code reviews
   - Direct account changes bypassing source control
2. Manual sandbox-to-production migration is time-consuming and error-prone
3. Risk of uploading to wrong accounts with no systematic prevention
4. Easy to overwrite others' changes without enforced checks
5. No clear implementation path for TypeScript, linting, or testing

## Proposed Solution

### Repository Structure
- One repo per client with dedicated branches:
  - `main` - Production account code
  - `dev` - Development sandbox code
  - `test` - Test sandbox code (when applicable)
- Restricted push access to `main` branch - requires PR approval
- Elimination of separate Production/Sandbox folders in favor of branch separation

### Development Process
The daily development workflow remains largely unchanged:
1. Work in `dev` branch
2. Pull latest changes
3. Make and upload changes to dev sandbox
4. Get code review
5. Commit and push to `dev`

### Automated Deployment Flow
When ready to deploy to production:
1. Create PR from `dev` to `main`
2. System automatically:
   - Compares current account code with last deployment
   - Identifies conflicts from direct account changes
   - Runs optional tests/linting
3. Required code review
4. Upon approval and passing checks, merge triggers automated deployment:
   - Re-runs conflict checks
   - Deploys via ACP including SuiteScript files and objects
   - Aborts if conflicts detected

## Benefits
### Developer Productivity
Eliminates manual:
- Code copying between folders
- File comparisons and uploads
- Script record/deployment configuration

### Error Prevention
Prevents common issues:
- Missed file uploads
- Pre-upload file comparisons
- Wrong account uploads
- Script record misconfigurations

### Client Value
- More reliable deployments
- Faster turnaround time
- Increased confidence in customization services

## Technical Implementation Details

### Platform Comparison

| Bitbucket Pipelines | Mint CI/CD |
|---------------------|------------|
| Existing access | Requires new RWX accounts |
| Limited caching | Comprehensive caching |
| 2500/3500 monthly build minutes | Pay-per-second billing |
| Requires custom docker images | No custom images needed |
| Native BitBucket integration | Requires GitHub integration |

### Platform Recommendation
Mint CI/CD is recommended because:
- Better caching reduces deployment time
- No Docker image maintenance
- More cost-effective with pay-per-second billing
- More reliable than current BitBucket Pipeline attempts

### GitHub Integration
While Mint lacks BitBucket integration, we can:
1. Add GitHub remote to existing repos
2. Use GitHub for deployment PRs
3. Consider full GitHub migration if successful due to:
   - Faster server response
   - Better PR blocking capabilities
   - Native Mint integration

### Permission Management
- Restrict `main` branch pushes via BitBucket/GitHub
- Grant exception access to senior developers for urgent fixes
- Consider revoking direct production token access to enforce process
```

This version maintains the clear structure while providing enough context for decision-makers to understand:
- The current process and its problems
- How the new process works
- Why specific technical choices are recommended
- Implementation considerations and challenges
